sections.html:
Loveland is a home rule city in southeastern Larimer County, about 46 miles north of the Colorado State Capitol in Denver. It is the second most populous municipality in Larimer County and the 14th most populous city in Colorado.

The city sits at the base of the Front Range foothills, just east of the mouth of Big Thompson Canyon, where U.S. Highway 34 meets U.S. Highway 287. Fort Collins, the county seat, lies to the north, and the two cities have grown toward each other, with county-owned open space set aside in the 1990s as a buffer. Loveland's northern limits now touch Windsor, which has spread west across Interstate 25.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Loveland's housing?
sections.html:
Loveland was founded in 1877 along the new Colorado Central Railroad, near its crossing of the Big Thompson River, and was named for the railroad's president, William A. H. Loveland. Earlier, Mariano Medina had built Fort Namaqua in 1858 as a trading post and stage station, on a site that is now Namaqua Park.

For the first half of the twentieth century the town lived on farming, mostly sugar beets and sour cherries. The Great Western Sugar Company built a factory here in 1901 and kept it running until 1977. By the late 1920s Spring Glade Orchard was the largest cherry orchard west of the Mississippi, producing more than $1 million of cherries a year, until drought, blight, competition and a killer freeze ended the industry.

The economy then diversified with plants run by Hewlett-Packard, Teledyne and Hach, and later with a large medical center. Population jumped from 16,220 in 1970 to 30,215 in 1980 and 76,378 in 2020, which means Loveland has houses from several building booms.

Two historic floods hit the Big Thompson watershed within living memory, and both are part of the local conversation about property.

  • The Big Thompson Flood of 1976 killed 144 people, with five bodies never found. The USGS and the Colorado Department of Natural Resources treat it as roughly a 1-in-500-year event.
  • The flood of September 12, 2013 followed four days of heavy rain. Sections of U.S. Highway 34, the main road to Estes Park, collapsed, and two people died in Larimer County. Loveland itself received about 4 inches of rain, far less than the mountains upstream.

If you own near the river, ask the city or county whether your parcel is mapped in a floodplain. A buyer, lender or insurer will ask the same thing, and knowing the answer early keeps a sale from stalling.

Loveland's location on U.S. 34, a main access route to Estes Park and Rocky Mountain National Park, brings steady tourist traffic in summer. The city also works as a bedroom community, with residents commuting to Fort Collins, Greeley, Boulder, Westminster and other parts of the Denver area.

The city has pushed its limits east to the I-25 and U.S. 34 interchange, an area known as Centerra, which has become a commercial hub for northern Colorado. It includes a shopping center, a large medical center and the Blue Arena. The interchange is shared with Johnstown in Weld County.

Loveland also has a distinct cultural side. There are three foundries, an art museum and an annual August sculpture show, and the city's public art collection holds 475 pieces, with more than 150 in the Benson Sculpture Garden. Each year the city re-mails valentines from around the world, a program that began in 1947 and handles more than 160,000 cards.

sections.h2: Which schools and transit options serve Loveland?
sections.html:
Public schools are run by the Thompson R2-J School District. High schools in the city include Loveland High School, Mountain View High School, Thompson Valley High School, Harold Ferguson High School and Loveland Classical High School. Aims Community College and a Northern Colorado Center of Colorado Christian University offer continuing education.

  • COLT, the City of Loveland Transit system, runs local buses.
  • FLEX connects Loveland with Fort Collins, Berthoud and Longmont.
  • Bustang express buses link the city with Denver.
  • The Poudre Express connects Loveland with Greeley and Windsor.
  • The Fort Collins/Loveland Airport serves corporate and general aviation but has no commercial airline service, so Denver International Airport, about 70 miles south, is the nearest commercial option.

Interstate 25, U.S. 34, U.S. 287 and State Highways 60 and 402 are the main roads through the city.

sections.h2: What does Loveland's climate mean for your roof and yard?
sections.html:
Loveland is classed as humid continental in some references and cold semi-arid in others, with warm to hot summers and long, moderately cold winters that are sometimes severe. Average snowfall is 47 inches a year.

Snow load, freeze and thaw cycles and summer heat all wear on roofs, gutters and exterior paint. If your house has a deferred roof or a tired furnace, price those items before you list. Lake Loveland, an early irrigation reservoir inside city limits, is another local detail: public fishing is available from public shorelines, but recreation rights on the lake belong to the homeowners whose lots surround it.

sections.h2: How do Larimer County valuation and tax dates affect a Loveland sale?
sections.html:
Larimer County reappraises all real property on a two-year cycle in odd-numbered years, and owners received a Notice of Valuation in May 2025. The Assessor's Office can be reached at (970) 498-7050 to discuss a value.

The payment schedule follows the statewide pattern used by Colorado treasurers. Adams County, for example, lists a first-half payment on February 28, a second half on June 15 and a full payment on April 30, and Colorado taxes are collected one year in arrears. Confirm the exact dates for Larimer County with its treasurer, and ask your closing agent how the current year's tax will be handled at the table.

Colorado also charges a state documentary fee of 1 cent per $100 on transfers above $500, and every recorded deed needs the buyer's mailing address. Both rules are described on Weld County's recording page and come from state law.

Loveland runs under a home rule, council-manager form of government. A nine-member city council, led by a mayor elected to a two-year term, sets policy, and each of the city's four wards elects two council members to four-year terms.

Permits, code questions and utility accounts for a Loveland address go through the city, so start there when you need to confirm what a buyer will ask about the property.

sections.h2: What should a Loveland seller know before choosing a sale route?
sections.html:
A Loveland house can be listed, sold by the owner or sold for cash, and each route trades time against effort. A listing brings the widest buyer pool but also repairs, showings and inspection negotiations. A cash sale is faster and usually as-is.

If the house is inherited, rented out or behind on payments, say so up front. Those details change the paperwork more than the price conversation does, and our team can walk through them with you before you decide anything.

faqs.q: What county is Loveland, CO in?
faqs.a: Loveland is in southeastern Larimer County. The county seat is Fort Collins, and the Larimer County Assessor handles valuation for Loveland homes.

faqs.q: How often does Larimer County reappraise homes?
faqs.a: Every two years, in odd-numbered years. Owners received a Notice of Valuation in May 2025.
Loveland is near the Big Thompson River, which flooded severely in 1976 and again in 2013. Ask the city or county whether your specific parcel is in a mapped floodplain.
The Thompson R2-J School District runs Loveland's public schools.

faqs.q: Does Loveland have an airport with commercial flights?
faqs.a: No. The Fort Collins/Loveland Airport handles corporate and general aviation only, and Denver International Airport is about 70 miles away.
